issues.legal_issue: Issues concerning execution proceedings that have been finally determined cannot be reopened through later objections in the same execution.
material_facts: The objections to the auction sale, its confirmation, the sale certificate, and the compromise were rejected by the executing court and the resulting decisions were upheld on appeal; a further challenge was dismissed.
A later order rejecting objections, including the contention that the compromise had adjusted the decree, was not appealed.
The judgment debtor raised previously decided matters again when resisting delivery of possession.
issues.conclusion: The previously determined issues had attained finality and could not be re-agitated in later execution proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: A judicial determination that has attained finality binds the parties, and repeating the same challenge in later proceedings is impermissible and may amount to abuse of process. The court applied this principle to the earlier determinations concerning the execution sale, the compromise, and the alleged adjustment of the decree, including the contention under Order XXI Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is an objection or other proceeding arising during execution of a decree.
predicates.issue_previously_decided_finally: A court has already decided the issue and that decision has become final between the parties.
predicates.later_objection_repeats_issue: A party raises the same issue again in a later objection or proceeding.

issues.definition: When an issue in an execution proceeding has already been finally decided and a later objection repeats it, that issue cannot be reopened.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court is not required to remand a case solely because the lower court gave no reasons, and may decide the merits itself where appropriate.
material_facts: The Single Judge dismissed the appeal without giving reasons.
The Division Bench considered the merits and declined to remit the matter for a fresh decision.
The litigation had continued for many years, and remand would have prolonged it further.
issues.conclusion: The Division Bench acted within its discretion by deciding the appeal on the merits instead of remanding it, and its approach did not warrant interference.
issues.legal_principle: Courts and authorities exercising adjudicatory power should give reasons: reasons demonstrate application of mind, reduce arbitrariness, promote transparency and fairness, and assist appellate review. Hindustan Times Limited v. Union of India, Arun s/o Mahadeorao Damka v. Addl. Inspector General of Police, Union of India v. Jai Prakash Singh, Secretary and Curator, Victoria Memorial Hall v. Howrah Ganatantrik Nagrik Samity, Ram Phal v. State of Haryana, and Director, Horticulture Punjab v. Jagjivan Parshad support the requirement to give reasons. However, absence of reasons in an appealable order does not impose an inflexible duty to remand: whether to remit or decide the merits is for the appellate court to determine, having regard to the nature of the dispute, the evidence and issues involved, and whether remand would unnecessarily prolong litigation.

predicates.appeal_from_unreasoned_order: A party brings an appeal from a lower court's order that gives no reasons.
predicates.appellate_court_can_determine_merits: The appellate court is able to examine and decide the merits of the dispute.
predicates.remand_would_prolong_litigation: Sending the matter back would unnecessarily extend the litigation.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an order without reasons, the appellate court can determine the merits, and remand would prolong litigation, the appellate court may decide the merits without remanding.
